title: Because it was he
hookLine: Montaigne on his friend La Boétie: because it was he, because it was I (Essays 1.28)

cards: Two men in France have heard about each other for a while, and each is curious about the other. Then, by chance, they meet at a great feast, in the middle of a crowd.
By the end of that first meeting, one of them later wrote, they were so taken with each other that nothing was ever again as close to either of them as the other. The writer was Michel de Montaigne.
The friend was Étienne de La Boétie. The essay is called, simply, Of Friendship.

teach.b: First, the question he can't answer. If someone pressed him to say why he loved his friend, Montaigne says, he could only answer: because it was he, because it was I. No list of reasons, no virtues counted up.
Second, the seam disappears. In this friendship, the two souls were so mingled that the seam joining them couldn't be found.
He sets it apart from what he calls common friendships, where you walk with the bridle in your hand, with prudence and caution.
In theirs, everything was held in common, so neither could even be said to give the other anything.
Third, cut short. La Boétie died, and the friendship ended far sooner than Montaigne wanted. Set beside the time he had with his friend, he writes, the rest of his life was smoke, a long dark night.
Fourth, against the list. Two days ago Aristotle explained friendship by what it rests on, and yesterday by its marks. Montaigne doesn't throw that out.
But he insists a friendship like this can't be fully explained from the outside. You can describe it; you can't give its reasons. The reason is the person, two names and nothing else.

how: Montaigne's essay Of Friendship, from the first book of his Essays, is read in literature and philosophy courses, and some readers turn to it when they're grieving a friend.

o: the French essayist who wrote Of Friendship
the friend whose early death ended the bond
a Greek thinker who listed friendship's marks

s: Montaigne gives a list of reasons he loved his friend
his answer is: because it was he, because it was I.
the two had heard of each other before they met
then they met by chance at a great feast.
Montaigne says every friendship is like this one
he sets it apart from common friendships.

games.q: you're Montaigne. someone presses you: why did you love your friend? what do you answer?
o: list his virtues, one by one.
because it was he, because it was I.
because he was useful to me.
games.why: no reasons at all. in his words, the friendship could only be explained by the two people in it.

practice: Let your deepest friendship come to mind, whether it's going on now, or faded, or lost to death, and don't explain it: just let their face, their voice, something they used to say be there.
If reasons arrive, let them pass by, and rest in the plain fact of them. If no friendship like that comes, let the one you'd hope for sit there instead, without a face yet.

wordCard.voice: Montaigne, who said he loved his friend because it was he, because it was I, with no list of reasons to give. Today's word.
